title: The Islamic Dilemma: A Fair Guide for Doubters
excerpt: The Islamic dilemma says the Qur'an affirms a Bible that contradicts it. A calm, fair guide for doubters: the argument, the classical answers, the limits.
body:
If you met the Islamic dilemma in a video, a comment thread or a debate clip, you probably met the Islamic dilemma as a trap: two doors, both said to lead out of Islam. This guide is for the person who saw it and could not stop thinking about it. It sets out the Islamic dilemma as its proponents make it, gives the classical Muslim answers, and is honest about where each side is strong. You do not need to have settled anything to read it.

One thing first. Being shaken by the Islamic dilemma is not a sin and not a sign that something is wrong with you. The Prophet's Companions told him they found thoughts in themselves they could hardly bring themselves to speak, and he told them that this was clear faith (Muslim 132). A question that frightens you is still a question, and it can be looked at calmly.

What the Islamic dilemma says

The Islamic dilemma is an argument made popular by Christian apologists, among them James White and David Wood, in debates and online videos. In its usual form it runs like this. The Qur'an speaks well of the Torah and the Gospel. It says it was sent down "confirming what was before it" (3:3). It tells the people of the Gospel to judge by what God revealed in it (5:47). It tells the People of the Book that they stand on nothing until they uphold the Torah and the Gospel (5:68). It even tells the Prophet, if he is in doubt, to ask those who read the Scripture before him (10:94).

From there the Islamic dilemma offers two options. If the Torah and Gospel the Qur'an affirms are the Bible Christians and Jews read today, then the Qur'an is contradicted by them, most obviously on the crucifixion and the divinity of Jesus. If instead those books were corrupted, then the Qur'an affirmed corrupted books, or failed to notice that they were. Either way, the argument concludes, the Qur'an is wrong, and Islam fails.

That is a fair summary, and the Islamic dilemma is cleverly built: it uses the Qur'an's own words, asks a real question, and fits in a single sentence, which is why the Islamic dilemma travels so well online.

Why the Islamic dilemma feels so strong online

The Islamic dilemma works by making you accept two options before you have checked whether they are the only ones. In a ninety-second clip on the Islamic dilemma there is no time to ask what the Qur'an means by "the Torah" and "the Gospel", or whether "confirming" means "vouching for every word of a later book". The format rewards the person who asks the question and punishes the person who needs a paragraph to answer it.

That is a description of the medium, not an accusation against those who present the Islamic dilemma. This site has written about how online argument shapes what feels convincing, in the polemical echo chamber and in the doubt websites confirmed my doubts. With the Islamic dilemma, the useful habit is simple: before choosing a door, check the walls.

What "Tawrat" and "Injil" mean in the Qur'an

The first answer to the Islamic dilemma is about words, and it is the one most often skipped in debates about the Islamic dilemma. When the Qur'an says Tawrat, it means the revelation God gave to Moses. When it says Injil, it means the revelation God gave to Jesus: "We gave him the Gospel, in which was guidance and light" (5:46). It speaks of the Injil in the singular, as something given to Jesus, not as four biographies written about him by others.

The Bible as Christians hold it is a different kind of object. The Gospels of Matthew, Mark, Luke and John are accounts of Jesus' life composed after his ministry, and the New Testament also contains letters, including those of Paul of Tarsus, and other writings, gathered into a canon over the following centuries. Whether those books preserve the Injil given to Jesus, in part or in whole, is exactly the question. The Islamic dilemma assumes the answer at the start, by treating "the Gospel" in 5:47 as a name for the New Testament. The sister site apostleofdoom.org takes up that assumption in detail, in its piece on Paul and the Islamic dilemma.

The classical scholars did not hold that every word in the Bible is false, and they did not hold that every word in it is the Injil. Ibn Taymiyya, in al-Jawab al-Sahih, reports a range of Muslim views and says that the view that the altered wording is a small part is the more evident one, while adding that alteration in the Gospels is more evident than in the Torah, and that many hold the Injil which is God's speech is not these Gospels.1 That nuanced position is not one of the two doors the Islamic dilemma offers.

Muhaymin: the Qur'an as a guardian over earlier scripture

The verse the Islamic dilemma quotes most, 5:48, says more than "confirming". It says God sent down the Book "confirming that which preceded it of the Scripture and as a criterion over it". The Arabic word rendered "criterion" is muhaymin. Ibn Kathir collects the early explanations: a trustee, a witness, a judge over the books before it. He reports Ibn Jurayj's gloss that the Qur'an is a trustee over the earlier books, so that what agrees with it in them is true and what differs from it is false, and he says the explanations all come to the same thing.2

This matters for the Islamic dilemma. A book that confirms earlier scripture and also stands as a check on it is not claiming that every copy in circulation is intact. It is claiming that the earlier revelation was true, and that the Qur'an is the measure by which later readers can tell what survives of it. One may disagree with that claim. But it is a third option to the Islamic dilemma, stated in the very verse the Islamic dilemma cites.

Tahrif: changed meaning or changed words?

The Qur'an accuses some of the People of the Book of tahrif, distorting "words from their places" (4:46; 5:13), of hearing God's words and distorting them after understanding them (2:75), and of writing a book with their own hands and calling it God's (2:79). Muslim scholars have long distinguished two kinds of tahrif: tahrif al-ma'na, distorting the meaning by interpretation, and tahrif al-lafz, changing the wording itself.

Both positions have classical defenders, and both bear on the Islamic dilemma. In the chapter headings of Sahih al-Bukhari, a gloss explains yuharrifun as "they remove", then says that no one removes the wording of any of God's books, but they distort it by interpreting it otherwise than it should be.3 At the other end, Ibn Hazm in al-Fisal argued at length, passage by passage, that the Torah in circulation in his day was altered.4 Ibn Taymiyya took a middle course: Muslims do not claim that every copy in the world, in every language, was altered since the Prophet's time; some wording was changed and much was changed in meaning.5

For the Islamic dilemma, the point is that "corrupted" is not one thing. The second door says that if the books were corrupted, the Qur'an affirmed corrupted books. But no classical scholar held that the Qur'an affirmed whatever later copies contain. They held that it affirmed the revelation, and warned that people had changed its meaning, its wording, or both.

"Let the people of the Gospel judge": reading 5:47 and 5:68

The strongest form of the Islamic dilemma rests on 5:47: "let the People of the Gospel judge by what God has revealed therein." If the Gospel was lost, how could they judge by it? Ibn Kathir records that the verse was read in two ways. In one reading it is a command: let them judge by it. In the other it describes a purpose: We gave him the Gospel so that its people might judge by it, in their own time.6 On the second reading the verse describes what the Gospel was given for, and the Islamic dilemma loses its premise.

Ibn Kathir also explains the command reading: the people of the Gospel were to believe all that is in it, including, as he says, its good news of a prophet to come, and to follow him when he appeared. That is how he connects 5:47 with 5:68, the other verse at the heart of the Islamic dilemma, which tells the People of the Book they stand on nothing until they uphold the Torah, the Gospel and "what has been revealed to you from your Lord".6 On this reading, upholding the earlier scripture means accepting what it pointed to, not using it to overrule the Qur'an.

There is also a report in Abu Dawud, graded hasan by al-Albani, in which a group of Jews brought the Torah to the Prophet in a case of adultery; he placed it on a cushion and said, "I believe in you and in the One who revealed you".7 The respect shown to the Torah there is real, and it fits the classical view: honour the revelation, and judge what has been done with it.

10:94: "ask those who read the Scripture"

Presentations of the Islamic dilemma often close with 10:94: if you are in doubt, ask those who have been reading the Scripture before you. The verse ends: "The truth has certainly come to you from your Lord, so never be among the doubters." It is addressed to the Prophet, it is conditional, and it points to the People of the Book as witnesses to something specific, that earlier revelation and earlier prophets were real. It does not tell Muslims to treat later scripture as the judge of the Qur'an.

The Prophet's own instruction is preserved in al-Bukhari. When the People of the Book read the Torah in Hebrew and explained it in Arabic, he said: "Do not believe the People of the Book and do not disbelieve them, but say: We believe in God and what was sent down to us".8 For the Islamic dilemma that is a third door again: neither blanket acceptance nor blanket rejection, but caution about a text whose transmission one cannot check.

Where the Islamic dilemma is weak, and where it has a point

Put together, the classical answers to the Islamic dilemma make the same move. The Islamic dilemma says the Qur'an must either vouch for today's Bible or condemn the revelation it praises. The scholars said the Qur'an praises the revelation given to Moses and Jesus, stands as a guardian over it, and accuses later communities of changing its meaning and, in some places, its words. That is a coherent position, and it is not caught by either horn of the Islamic dilemma.

Fairness asks us to say what the Islamic dilemma gets right. It is right that Muslims sometimes answer the Islamic dilemma badly, by saying the Bible is "all corrupt" in one breath and quoting it as evidence for Muhammad in the next. It is right that the meaning of 5:47 and 5:68 needs explaining rather than waving away. And it is right that a reader is owed the reasons, not a slogan. Compelling Evidence sets out the textual argument at more length in the Islamic dilemma: the Qur'an and the Bible, and bestofislam.org gives a clear Muslim answer to the Islamic dilemma for general readers.

If the Islamic dilemma has shaken you

You may have read all of this and still feel unsettled by the Islamic dilemma. That is allowed. An argument can stay with you long after you understand the reply. Our guide on how to assess a doubt offers a way of taking a question apart without being swept along by it, and doubt and the inner life looks at how al-Ghazali lived through a much deeper crisis than one debate clip.

The Islamic dilemma is rarely only an intellectual question. If the Islamic dilemma reached you while you were already struggling, with family, with faith, with your own mind, please do not carry it alone. Our page on where to find support lists ways to reach help. If you are in danger or thinking of harming yourself, contact your local emergency number now.

You may also find it useful to read believe without knowing and why this religion and not another, which deal with the wider question the Islamic dilemma often opens.

Questions readers ask about the Islamic dilemma

Does the Qur'an say the Bible is preserved? No verse says that the Bible as it exists today is preserved. The Qur'an praises the Torah and the Injil as revelations and accuses some later communities of distorting them. The Islamic dilemma needs the first claim, and the Qur'an does not make it.

Is the Islamic dilemma a new argument? The modern form of the Islamic dilemma is recent, but the underlying question is old. Ibn Taymiyya's al-Jawab al-Sahih was written in the fourteenth century in reply to a Christian letter making related points, and Ibn Hazm took up the question two centuries earlier.

Is it wrong to find the Islamic dilemma persuasive? No. Finding the Islamic dilemma persuasive is an experience, not a choice. What you do next, reading, asking, waiting, is up to you.

The Islamic dilemma across the network

  • Abrahamic Religions: the Islamic dilemma in the setting of all three Abrahamic scriptures.
  • Injil.help: the pillar page on what the Injil is, and why it matters to the argument.
  • Compelling Evidence: the textual case on the Qur'an and the Bible, at length.
  • Best of Islam: a clear Muslim answer for general readers.
  • Apostle of Doom: which Injil the Qur'an affirms, and Paul's place in the New Testament canon.
  • Lailatul Qadar: the Qur'an sent down "confirming what came before it", and what muhaymin means.

title: What Apostasy (Riddah) Is in Islamic Law
excerpt: What classical Islamic law means by apostasy (riddah): the definition, the conditions of adulthood, sanity and free choice, and why doubt is not apostasy.
body:
This guide explains what classical Islamic law means by apostasy, in Arabic riddah or irtidad, and the conditions the jurists attached to it. It describes the law as the scholars wrote it. It does not advocate anything, and it is not a ruling about you. If you are reading because you are frightened about your own situation, please read the section near the end first, and know that doubting is not apostasy in any school of law.

The word and the definition

The Arabic root r-d-d means to turn back or return. The Qur'an uses the verb for turning back from one's religion: "whoever of you turns back from his religion and dies while a disbeliever, their deeds have become worthless in this world and the Hereafter" (2:217). The person who does so is the murtadd, the one who has turned back, which is where this site takes its name.

The jurists gave a short definition. Ibn Qudama, the Hanbali jurist of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, opens the chapter on the apostate in al-Mughni with it: the apostate is the one who returns from the religion of Islam to disbelief.1 Every school uses a definition of this kind. What matters in practice is not the one-line definition but the conditions, because the conditions decide who the definition can apply to.

The conditions: who can be an apostate in law

The classical schools agree on a set of conditions before a person can be treated as an apostate. They are stated in different words in different books, but their substance is shared.

Adulthood. The person must have reached legal maturity. Ibn Qudama's statement of the rule begins with an apostate "who is adult and of sound mind".1 A child's words do not have this legal effect.

Sound mind. The person must be sane. The insane are outside legal responsibility altogether. The jurists debated cases at the edge of this condition, such as a person who is intoxicated. Ibn Qudama reports that the Hanbali school has two narrations from Ahmad on this, and that Abu Hanifa held that the apostasy of the intoxicated is not valid, because it depends on belief and intention and the intoxicated person has neither.2

Free choice. A person forced to say words of disbelief is not an apostate. The Qur'an makes the exception itself: "except for one who is forced while his heart is secure in faith" (16:106). The same principle runs the other way. Ibn Qudama discusses a non-Muslim under protection who is forced to accept Islam, and holds that the conversion has no legal effect, because he was compelled to something it is forbidden to compel, citing "there is no compulsion in religion" (2:256).3

Knowledge and intention. The jurists distinguished between a person who knowingly rejects something known to be part of the religion and a person who is ignorant, mistaken, or interpreting. They spent a great deal of ink on how to treat people who held wrong beliefs through interpretation, and many declined to declare them outside Islam. Ibn Qudama notes, for example, that most jurists did not declare the Kharijites unbelievers, even though they shed Muslim blood believing it lawful.4

What counts as apostasy, and what does not

The legal manuals list the acts and statements by which a person might leave Islam: explicitly renouncing it, denying God or a prophet, denying something known by everyone to be part of the religion, or mocking God or the Qur'an. These lists are long, and reading them out of context is frightening. Read in context, three things stand out.

First, the lists describe a deliberate act by a responsible person. They are not lists of thoughts. Islamic law does not hold people to account for what passes through their minds. The Prophet told Companions troubled by thoughts they could hardly speak that this was clear faith (Muslim 132), and he said that deeds are judged by intentions (al-Bukhari 1).5

Second, the jurists treated declaring a Muslim an unbeliever, takfir, as a grave matter to be approached with caution. The manuals show that caution in many places. In a related case, a non-Muslim who pronounced the testimony of faith and then said he had not meant to enter Islam, Ibn Qudama reports Ahmad's view that a person's statement is accepted where it may be true, "so his blood is not shed on a doubt".6

Third, doubt is not on the list. Asking questions, reading criticism, struggling to pray, feeling far from God: none of these is apostasy in any school. The tradition has a long and honest literature on doubt, which our guide doubt and the inner life describes, and the companion site's article on whether doubt is permitted in Islam sets out the case.

Who decides

In the classical law, apostasy is a matter for a court, not for individuals. The jurist applies the conditions; a family member, an imam or a stranger on the internet has no standing to declare anyone an apostate with legal effect. Ibn Qudama says plainly that if anyone other than the ruler kills an apostate he has done wrong and is to be punished for overstepping.7 Whatever one thinks of the classical penalty, which our guide the apostasy penalty discusses, the classical law never licensed private violence.

The jurists also required that the person be invited to return. The schools differed over how long, which the penalty guide sets out. The point here is that the law, as written, treated the matter as one requiring due process, conditions and time.

The consequences the jurists discussed

Besides the penal question, the manuals discuss civil consequences: what happens to a marriage, to property, to inheritance. Ibn Qudama records, for instance, a disagreement over whether the property of an apostate passes to heirs at once, as Abu Hanifa held, or is held in trust while the person may still return.8 These questions still matter, because in several modern states personal status law, not criminal law, is where apostasy has its effect. Our guide leaving and the law sets out where that is so.

Riddah in history

The word riddah is also the name of a historical event: the wars fought by the first caliph, Abu Bakr, against tribes that withdrew from the young Muslim polity after the Prophet's death, some of them refusing to pay the alms tax and some following rival claimants to prophethood. Those wars were about political allegiance and armed secession as much as belief, and modern scholars who argue that the classical penalty concerned treason rather than private conscience often begin there. The companion site discusses this history in the political history of apostasy, and this site's rebuttal apostasy and the classical law sets out the legal position in brief.

What the Qur'an itself says

The Qur'an speaks about turning away from faith several times and in serious terms. It warns that the deeds of one who dies in disbelief are lost (2:217). It speaks of those who believe and disbelieve repeatedly (4:137). It promises wrath to those who open their breasts to disbelief willingly (16:106). But no verse of the Qur'an prescribes a worldly penalty for apostasy. The penalties it describes are in the Hereafter, and alongside them stand verses on choice: "there is no compulsion in religion" (2:256), and "whoever wills, let him believe; and whoever wills, let him disbelieve" (18:29). How these verses relate to the hadith on which the classical penalty rests is the heart of the modern debate.

The Qur'an also leaves the door open. The passage that begins by asking how God will guide a people who disbelieved after believing continues: "except for those who repent after that and correct themselves; indeed God is Forgiving and Merciful" (3:89). Our guide coming back is about that door.

If you are reading this about yourself

Please read this slowly. Nothing in the paragraphs above describes a person who is unsure. Doubt is not apostasy. Having questions is not apostasy. Reading this site is not apostasy. Even in the classical law, apostasy required an adult of sound mind, acting freely and knowingly, and a court. No one has the right to apply that law to you privately, and anyone who threatens you is doing something the classical jurists themselves condemned.

If you have decided you no longer believe, that is a serious matter for you, and it may carry real risks depending on where you live and who is around you. Those risks are real, and this site does not pretend otherwise. Read afraid of what happens if I leave, and if you are in any danger, look at where to find support. If you are in immediate danger, contact your local emergency number.

Whatever you have decided, you deserve accurate information rather than threats, and you deserve time. This guide has tried to give you the first. The second is yours to take.

Summary

  • Apostasy, riddah, is defined in classical law as turning back from Islam to disbelief.
  • It applies only to an adult of sound mind, acting freely and knowingly. Compulsion removes it entirely (16:106).
  • Thoughts, doubts and questions are not apostasy.
  • Only a court could apply the classical law, and private violence was condemned by the jurists themselves.
  • The Qur'an prescribes no worldly penalty for apostasy, and it keeps the door of return open (3:89).

title: The Apostasy Penalty: Evidence and Debate
excerpt: The apostasy penalty in Islamic law: the hadith evidence, the classical positions, and the modern scholarly debate, set out neutrally with sources.
body:
Few subjects frighten a doubting Muslim more than the apostasy penalty, and few are discussed online with less care. This guide sets out the evidence the classical jurists relied on, the positions they took, and the modern debate among Muslim scholars, as neutrally as it can. It quotes the sources and names who said what. It does not advocate a position, and it is not a ruling about anyone. If you are reading this because you are afraid for yourself, please read the last section first.

The evidence in the hadith

The Qur'an warns of loss in the Hereafter for those who turn back from faith (2:217; 16:106) but prescribes no worldly penalty for apostasy. The classical penalty rests on hadith. Three reports carry most of the weight.

"Whoever changes his religion, kill him." Al-Bukhari reports through 'Ikrima that 'Ali burned some people described as zanadiqa, heretics. Ibn 'Abbas, hearing of it, said that he would not have burned them, because the Prophet forbade punishing with fire, but that he would have killed them, because the Prophet said: "whoever changes his religion, kill him".1 The report appears twice in al-Bukhari, nos. 3017 and 6922.

"Except in one of three cases." Al-Bukhari and Muslim report from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud that the blood of a Muslim who testifies to God's oneness and the Prophet's message is not lawful except in one of three cases: a life for a life, the married adulterer, and, in al-Bukhari's wording, "the one who leaves the religion, abandoning the community".2 Muslim's wording is "the one who abandons his religion, separating from the community".

The narration of 'A'isha. Abu Dawud reports the same saying through 'A'isha with a different third case: "a man who goes out to fight God and His Messenger; he is killed, or crucified, or exiled from the land". Al-Albani graded it sahih.3 This wording matters in the modern debate, as we will see.

Alongside these, the jurists cited the report in al-Bukhari in which Mu'adh ibn Jabal, arriving in Yemen, found a man bound in Abu Musa's presence, a Jew who had accepted Islam and then returned to Judaism, and refused to sit until he was killed, saying it was the judgement of God and His Messenger.4 And they knew the report, also in al-Bukhari, of a Bedouin who pledged allegiance to the Prophet in Medina, fell ill, asked three times to be released from his pledge, was refused, and left the city. The Prophet said that Medina is like a bellows that expels its impurity; the report mentions no pursuit or punishment.5 Scholars disagree about what that report shows.

The classical positions

Ibn Qudama, the Hanbali jurist, summarises the classical law in al-Mughni. He states that the scholars agreed on the obligation to kill the apostate, reporting it from Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Uthman, 'Ali, Mu'adh, Abu Musa, Ibn 'Abbas, Khalid and others, and calls it a consensus.6 That statement represents the dominant classical position in all four Sunni schools. A reader should know that it is the position the classical texts state, and this guide does not soften it.

Within that position there was real disagreement on details, and the details are not small.

Women. The Hanbali, Maliki and Shafi'i schools applied the penalty to men and women alike. Abu Hanifa held that a woman apostate is not killed, though she is compelled to return by imprisonment and beating, citing the Prophet's prohibition on killing women, and reasoning that since a woman is not killed for original disbelief she is not killed for disbelief that comes later.6

The invitation to return. Most jurists required that the apostate be invited to repent, istitaba, before any penalty. Ibn Qudama reports a three-day period from 'Umar, held by Malik, Ishaq and the Hanafis, and one of al-Shafi'i's two views. He also records the opposite view, that no invitation is required, from 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr and Tawus, and reported from al-Hasan.7 He narrates the report in which 'Umar, told that an apostate had been executed at once, asked why they had not held him for three days, fed him a loaf each day and invited him to repent, "perhaps he would repent".7

Al-Nakha'i. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, the early Kufan jurist, is reported to have held that the apostate is invited to repent indefinitely. Ibn Qudama notes that this leads to his never being killed, and rejects it as contrary to the Sunnah and the consensus.8 The report of al-Nakha'i's view is often cited in the modern debate. Ibn Qudama's rejection of it should be cited with it.

Due process. The classical law reserved the matter to the ruler and his courts. Ibn Qudama states that if anyone other than the ruler kills an apostate, he has done wrong and is to be punished.9 The classical law did not license private killing, and anyone who claims otherwise is departing from it.

How the classical jurists understood the ruling

Classical works offered more than one rationale. Some framed apostasy as a crime against God's right. The Hanafi argument about women, set out above, draws an analogy with the women of an enemy people, who were not killed in war, and so links the penalty to the law of war rather than to belief alone. The structure of the riddah wars under Abu Bakr, fought against tribes withdrawing allegiance from the Medinan polity, gave the ruling a strongly political setting. This site's rebuttal apostasy and the classical law notes Muhammad Hamidullah's view that it treated apostasy as politico-religious rebellion, and the companion site's article on the political history of apostasy follows that history.

The modern scholarly debate

In the modern period, Muslim scholars have argued openly about whether the classical penalty applies to a person who changes belief privately in a modern state. The positions fall roughly into three groups. The summaries below are short and the works should be read in full; the page references are listed as needing the owner's check.

Retaining the penalty, with distinctions. Yusuf al-Qaradawi, in Jarimat al-Ridda wa 'Uqubat al-Murtadd (1996), upheld the penalty in principle, but distinguished between an apostate who keeps his change of belief to himself and one who campaigns against Islam and its community, and argued that the gravest treatment concerns the second.

Limiting it to treason or rebellion. A number of scholars read the hadith in light of 'A'isha's narration, in which the third case is a man who goes out to fight God and His Messenger, and the phrase in Ibn Mas'ud's narration, "abandoning the community". On this reading the ruling concerned apostasy joined to armed rebellion or treason against the polity, not private belief. Mahmud Shaltut, Shaykh al-Azhar, argued in al-Islam 'Aqida wa Shari'a that a fixed penalty is not established by solitary reports and that disbelief in itself does not warrant killing; the ruling attaches to aggression against Muslims. Mohammad Hashim Kamali makes a related argument in Freedom of Expression in Islam (1997).

Rejecting a worldly penalty for belief. Abdullah Saeed and Hassan Saeed, in Freedom of Religion, Apostasy and Islam (2004), and Taha Jabir al-'Alwani, in Apostasy in Islam: A Historical and Scriptural Analysis (2011), argue that the Qur'an's affirmation of freedom of belief (2:256; 18:29; 10:99) governs the hadith, that the Prophet's own practice, including the Bedouin who left Medina, shows no penalty for change of belief alone, and that the classical ruling belongs to the confessional politics of its time.

Each group answers the others. Those who retain the penalty point to the claimed consensus and the general wording "whoever changes his religion". Those who limit or reject it point to the specific wording of the other narrations, the Qur'an's verses on choice, and the political setting. Both sides are Muslim scholars arguing from the same sources. Anyone who tells you that the argument is settled, in either direction, is reporting a preference.

What applies in practice

A reader's real question is usually not "what did Ibn Qudama write" but "what can happen to me". The answer depends on where you live. Most Muslim-majority states attach no criminal penalty to leaving Islam. A small number retain it in statute or in uncodified judicial practice, and several attach civil consequences to marriage, inheritance or identity documents. Our guide leaving and the law sets out the statutes by region. International human rights law protects the freedom to change one's religion: the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, article 18, and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, article 18, as the UN Human Rights Committee explained in its General Comment No. 22. The companion site discusses this in apostasy and international law.

Reading the hadith fairly

It is tempting, on both sides, to read only the report that suits you. The person who wants to frighten quotes "whoever changes his religion, kill him" and stops. The person who wants to reassure quotes 2:256 and stops. A fair reader holds all of them together: the general wording, the narrations that speak of abandoning the community and of armed rebellion, the report of the Bedouin who left, the claimed consensus and the dissent reported from al-Nakha'i, and the Qur'an's verses on choice. Our guide hadith grading explained explains how the scholars weigh reports, and the doubt the hadith about leaving answers the most common form of the question.

For the reader this is about

Doubting is an offence nowhere. Having questions is not apostasy in any school of law, and no legal provision in any country reaches a person who is unsure. Even the classical law as stated above required an adult of sound mind, acting freely, and a court, and condemned private violence.

That said, the danger some people face is real, and it more often comes from family or community pressure than from any court. If you are frightened, read afraid of what happens if I leave and what leaving actually costs, and look at where to find support. If you are in immediate danger, contact your local emergency number. Do not make decisions about disclosure while you are unsafe; your safety comes first.

title: How to Assess a Doubt
excerpt: A step-by-step way to examine a doubt about Islam calmly: name it, find its source, read the text in context, weigh both sides, and give it time.
body:
A doubt usually arrives all at once. You read a claim, or watch a clip, or hear a question from a friend, and suddenly something you never examined feels unsteady. This guide offers a way of slowing that moment down: a set of questions you can put to any doubt, whichever way it eventually points. It will not tell you what to conclude. It is a method for taking a doubt seriously without being carried away by it.

Before the method, a word about you. Having a doubt is not a moral failure. The Prophet's Companions came to him troubled by thoughts they could hardly bring themselves to speak, and he told them that this was clear faith (Muslim 132). He also told believers what to do when the chain of questions reaches "who created your Lord?": to seek refuge in God and stop there (al-Bukhari 3276).1 That second instruction is not a ban on thinking. It recognises that some questions are not arguments at all, but intrusive thoughts that feed on attention. Telling the two apart is the first step.

Step one: write the doubt down in one sentence

Doubts are often a cloud of feelings attached to a half-remembered claim. Write the doubt as a single sentence you could show to someone else. "The Qur'an contradicts science." "A hadith says apostates must be killed." "If God is good, why did that happen to me?" A sentence can be examined; a cloud cannot.

Then ask which kind of doubt it is. This site sorts doubts into four kinds, and the kind matters, because each needs a different approach.

  • Intellectual: an argument about evidence or reason, such as the existence of God or the reliability of a text.
  • Scriptural: a specific verse or hadith that troubles you, such as 4:34 or a hadith that seems inhumane.
  • Emotional: a grief, a hurt, or an experience of God's absence, such as I was hurt and nobody helped.
  • Identity: a question about belonging, family, or who you are, such as born into it.

An emotional doubt dressed up as an intellectual one will not be settled by an argument, and an intellectual doubt will not be settled by comfort. Be honest with yourself about which you have. Often it is more than one.

Step two: find the source

Where did the doubt come from? A book, a lecture, a video, a social media post, a conversation? The Qur'an gives a rule for news brought by an unreliable carrier: "if there comes to you a disobedient one with information, investigate, lest you harm a people out of ignorance" (49:6). The same rule applies whichever direction the information points.

Ask of the source: who made this claim first? Is it quoting a primary text, and if so, which one, with a reference you can check? Is it reporting a scholar's view, and if so, does it name the book? Does it have a reason to present the matter one way? This is not an attack on the source. A Muslim preacher who misquotes a hadith to reassure you fails the test as badly as a critic who misquotes it to alarm you.

Step three: check the primary text

Most doubts rest on a primary text: a verse, a hadith, a ruling. Go and read it yourself, in context.

For a verse of the Qur'an, read the verses before and after, and if possible a classical commentary. Our guide reading the Qur'an in context explains how. Many doubts about verses dissolve at the next verse; some do not, and those deserve real attention.

For a hadith, find which collection it is in, its number, and how it was graded. A hadith quoted without a source tells you very little. A hadith graded weak by the scholars of hadith themselves is not evidence of what the Prophet said. Our guide hadith grading explained sets out how the grades work, and why the same hadith may be graded differently by different scholars.

For a legal ruling, find which school held it, in which book, and whether other schools disagreed. Classical law is full of disagreement, and a ruling quoted as "Islam says" is often one view among several.

Step four: state the strongest form of the other side

This step is the hardest and the most useful. Before deciding, try to state the best answer to your doubt, in the form its most careful defenders would give it. Then try to state the best form of the doubt, as its most careful advocate would put it.

If you can only state one side well, you have not finished. That applies whether you are leaning towards belief or away from it. Online material is very good at presenting one side and very bad at presenting the other; this site has written about it in the polemical echo chamber. A good test is whether someone who disagrees with you would recognise your summary of their view.

Step five: ask what follows

Suppose the doubt is correct. What exactly follows? Often much less than it first seems. A weak hadith being weak tells you nothing about the Qur'an. A disagreement among scholars tells you that scholars disagreed, not that nothing is true. A Muslim behaving badly tells you about that Muslim. This is not a trick to make doubts go away; it is a way of seeing their real size.

Suppose instead the answer is correct. What follows then? Sometimes a doubt is answered and leaves behind a smaller question, and that smaller question is the real one.

The doubt Muslims cannot even agree and the rebuttal the slide from hadith to nothing are worked examples of this step.

Step six: notice the pattern

Doubts rarely come alone. One question leads to another, and after a while the sheer number can feel like evidence in itself. It is worth asking whether you have many separate doubts or one doubt appearing in many forms. A person who has been hurt by a community may find every argument against that community's faith persuasive; that is human, and it is not a sign of foolishness. But it is worth knowing.

The companion site's article did your heart leave before your head? looks at this honestly, and so does your doubts are not a disease.

Step seven: give it time

Doubts that arrive in a night are rarely settled in one. There is no deadline. You do not have to reach a conclusion this week, tell anyone anything, or make any decision while you are still examining a question. Al-Ghazali, one of the greatest scholars in Islamic history, described a period of radical doubt that lasted nearly two months, and a later crisis of about six months during which he could not teach; he came through both, and wrote about them. Our guide doubt and the inner life tells that story.

Taking time is not avoidance. It is how serious questions are handled in every field.

Step eight: talk to someone

Examining a doubt alone, at night, on a phone, is the hardest way to do it. If you can, talk to someone you trust: a knowledgeable friend, a scholar who will listen rather than lecture, a counsellor. If no one around you feels safe to talk to, that is important information about your situation, and you should take it seriously. Our guide where to find support suggests where to start.

When the doubt is about people

Some doubts are not about texts at all. They are about what Muslims have done: a teacher who was cruel, a community that turned away when you needed it, a scandal in the news. These doubts deserve to be taken seriously, because the harm behind them is often real. They also deserve to be named for what they are. The question "can this community be trusted?" is a different question from "is this religion true?", and both are legitimate. Our rebuttal the state of Muslims argument deals with the second. The first may need a different kind of help, and it is not disloyal to look for it.

When a doubt is something else

Sometimes what feels like a doubt is a symptom. Intrusive, repetitive thoughts that you cannot stop, that cause distress, and that return however often they are answered, can be a feature of anxiety or of obsessive-compulsive disorder, including the form sometimes called scrupulosity. They are not a judgement on your faith or your intelligence, and they respond to treatment. If this sounds like you, please speak to a doctor or a mental health professional. Answering such thoughts with more arguments tends to feed them.

And if a doubt has come with thoughts of harming yourself, please stop reading and contact your local emergency number or a crisis line now. A question about religion can wait. You matter more than any argument.

A checklist

  1. Write the doubt in one sentence, and name its kind.
  2. Find where it came from.
  3. Read the primary text in context, with its reference and grade.
  4. State the strongest form of both sides.
  5. Ask what actually follows if the doubt is right, and if it is wrong.
  6. Notice whether many doubts are one doubt.
  7. Give it time.
  8. Talk to someone safe.

None of these steps decides the outcome for you. They make sure that whatever you conclude, you concluded it, rather than a clip or a comment thread concluding it for you.

title: Hadith Grading Explained for Doubters
excerpt: How hadith were graded: isnad and matn, sahih, hasan, da'if and mawdu', why gradings differ, and five questions to ask of any hadith quoted at you.
body:
If you have doubts about Islam, you have probably met a hadith that troubled you, quoted in a video or a post with the words "it is in the authentic collections". This guide explains, for a reader who is not a specialist, how Muslim scholars graded hadith, what the grades mean, and what they do not mean. It will help you read a quoted hadith more carefully, whichever way your questions lead.

What a hadith is

A hadith is a report of what the Prophet said, did, or approved. Each report has two parts. The isnad is the chain of people who passed it on: "A told me that B told him that C heard the Prophet say". The matn is the text, what was reportedly said or done. Grading is the scholars' judgement on how likely it is that the text really goes back, through that chain, to the Prophet.

You can see both parts in the first hadith of Sahih al-Bukhari, "deeds are judged by intentions". Al-Bukhari heard it from al-Humaydi, who heard it from Sufyan, from Yahya ibn Sa'id al-Ansari, from Muhammad ibn Ibrahim al-Taymi, from 'Alqama ibn Waqqas, who heard 'Umar ibn al-Khattab say from the pulpit that he heard the Prophet say it.1 Every name in that list is a person whose life and reliability the hadith critics studied.

The main grades

Sahih (sound). A hadith whose chain is unbroken, whose narrators are all upright and precise in what they transmit, and which is free of hidden defects and of contradiction with stronger reports. This is the highest grade.

Hasan (good). A hadith that meets the conditions of sahih, except that one or more narrators are slightly less precise. A hasan hadith is accepted as evidence by most scholars.

Da'if (weak). A hadith that fails one or more conditions: a break in the chain, a narrator who is unreliable or unknown, or a defect. A weak hadith is not established as the Prophet's words. Scholars differed over whether weak hadith could be used for encouraging good deeds; they did not use them to establish law or belief.

Mawdu' (fabricated). A report that the critics judged to be invented and falsely attributed to the Prophet. They compiled whole books of these, so that people would know not to repeat them.

There are many finer terms. A collector may combine grades, as al-Tirmidhi often does. After the hadith "God accepts the repentance of His servant until the death rattle", for example, al-Tirmidhi writes "this hadith is hasan gharib", good, and also unusual in its chain.2 Gharib means that at some point in the chain only one narrator carries it. It is a description of the chain, not in itself a criticism: the "intentions" hadith above is carried by one narrator at several of its early links, and it is in both Sahih collections.

How narrators were judged

The grade of a hadith depends above all on its narrators, and the scholars built a discipline to judge them, called al-jarh wa al-ta'dil, criticism and validation. For each narrator they asked two questions. Was he upright, honest and careful in religion, so that he would not knowingly lie? And was he precise, so that what he passed on was what he had heard? A pious man with a poor memory failed the second test, and the critics said so plainly, however much they respected him.

They also asked whether each narrator could actually have met the person he claims to report from: whether their lifetimes and travels overlapped. A chain in which two names never met is broken, however reliable each name is. Biographical dictionaries recording dates, teachers, students and the critics' verdicts run to many volumes, and they are what make a grading checkable rather than a matter of opinion.

None of this makes the system infallible. It does mean that when a scholar grades a hadith, he is making a claim that other scholars can test against the same evidence, and they often did.

The collections, and what "authentic" means

The two collections of al-Bukhari and Muslim, called the Sahihayn, were compiled with the aim of including only sound hadith, and the scholarly tradition has held them in the highest regard. The four Sunan collections of Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah include reports of every grade, and their compilers sometimes note the weakness themselves.

So "it is in Abu Dawud" does not mean "it is sound". It means "Abu Dawud recorded it". To know its grade, you need a grading. This site follows the gradings of Muhammad Nasir al-Din al-Albani where scholars differ, because his gradings of the four Sunan are complete and widely available. For example, al-Albani graded sahih Abu Dawud's narration from 'A'isha on the three cases in which a Muslim's blood is lawful, and graded hasan the narration in which the Prophet placed the Torah on a cushion.3

It also does not follow that "it is in al-Bukhari" ends every question. Scholars, including classical scholars such as al-Daraqutni, criticised a small number of reports in the Sahihayn, usually on technical grounds about the chain. Those criticisms are part of the tradition, not an attack on it. Questions about meaning, about how a sound report is to be understood, remain open even when its chain is secure.

Why gradings sometimes differ

Two scholars can grade the same hadith differently, and this unsettles readers who expected a single answer. The differences have reasons. A scholar may know a supporting chain the other did not consider, which can raise a weak report to hasan. Scholars may judge a particular narrator differently, especially one whose memory declined late in life. And they may weigh an apparent contradiction with a stronger report differently.

Differences in grading are evidence that the system was a working discipline, argued over by people who cared about getting it right. They are not evidence that grading is arbitrary.

When were hadith written down?

A common doubt holds that hadith were only written down two centuries after the Prophet. The great collections were completed in the third Islamic century, but writing began much earlier. 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr reported that he wrote down what he heard from the Prophet, and that the Prophet told him to keep writing, "for nothing comes from it but truth" (Abu Dawud 3646, al-Albani: sahih). This site's rebuttal hadith and the two centuries gap takes the question further, and the doubt written down centuries later answers it briefly. The companion site's articles on hadith authenticity and hadith reliability give the longer case.

How to read a hadith that troubles you

When a hadith is quoted at you, ask five questions.

  1. Where is it? Which collection, which number? A quotation without a reference cannot be checked, and some widely quoted "hadith" are not in any collection.
  2. How is it graded? Look for a named grading. If scholars differ, note who said what.
  3. What is the full text? Quotations are often shortened. The full report may include the occasion, a question that prompted it, or a qualification.
  4. Are there other narrations? The same saying often comes in several wordings. The narrations of "the three cases" are an example: one wording speaks of "the one who leaves his religion, abandoning the community", another of "a man who goes out to fight God and His Messenger". Reading only one gives a partial picture. Our guide the apostasy penalty shows why this matters.
  5. How did the scholars understand it? A sound chain tells you the report is reliable. It does not tell you what it means or how it was applied; for that, read a commentary.

The doubt hadith contain inhumane things and the rebuttal were monkeys stoned for adultery are worked examples: in the second, a report is shown to be the words of a later narrator, not the Prophet, which changes everything about how it should be read. The companion site discusses selective use of embarrassing reports at more length.

A note on quotations in great books

Great scholars quoted reports in their works for many purposes, and a quotation in a famous book is not a grading. Al-Ghazali's Ihya', for instance, contains many reports of varying strength, and later hadith scholars wrote a whole book tracing and grading them, the Takhrij by al-'Iraqi. Respecting a scholar does not require treating every report he cites as sound; the scholars themselves did not.

What grading cannot do for you

Grading tells you how reliable a report is. It cannot tell you whether you will find it beautiful or difficult, and it cannot settle a question of faith on its own. A doubt about a hadith can be the start of a long and worthwhile study, or it can be the visible part of a deeper question about whether the Prophet was who Muslims say he was. If it is the second, a grading table will not reach it, and it is better to know that. Our guide how to assess a doubt may help you tell the difference.

Whatever you conclude, you are entitled to the facts about the texts, not to a slogan in either direction. The hadith scholars spent their lives making sure the facts could be checked. That is still the best use of their work.

title: Reading the Qur'an in Context
excerpt: How to read a verse of the Qur'an in context: the passage, the occasion of revelation, the whole Qur'an, the Prophet's explanation and language.
body:
Many doubts begin with a single verse of the Qur'an, quoted on its own: a verse about fighting, about women, about unbelievers. This guide explains how Muslim scholars have read verses in context, and how you can do the same, so that you can see what a verse says before deciding what you think of it. Context does not make every difficulty disappear, and this guide will not pretend that it does. But a verse read without its context is not yet a verse you have read.

Why context matters for any text

Every text means something within a setting: the sentences around it, the occasion it addresses, the conventions of its language. A line from a law, a letter or a poem can mean the opposite of what it seems when it is cut out. The Qur'an is no different, and in some ways it needs more care, because it was revealed over about twenty-three years, in response to changing events, and much of it addresses particular people in particular situations.

The Qur'an itself invites close reading: "Then do they not reflect upon the Qur'an? If it had been from other than God, they would have found within it much contradiction" (4:82). It also warns against a particular kind of selective reading. Of its own verses it says that some are precise, "the foundation of the Book", and others are open to more than one meaning, and that "those in whose hearts is deviation" follow the second kind, "seeking discord" (3:7). That warning applies to anyone who picks a verse to make a point, whatever the point is.

Layer one: the verses around it

The first and simplest context is the passage. Read at least the verses before and after, and ideally the whole section. A great many quoted verses change meaning at this first step.

The verse often quoted as "kill the polytheists wherever you find them" is 9:5. The verse before it exempts polytheists who kept their treaty and did not support anyone against the Muslims: "complete for them their treaty until their term" (9:4). The verse after it says that if any polytheist asks for protection, he is to be given it, so that he may hear the words of God, "then deliver him to his place of safety" (9:6). Whatever one concludes about the passage, it is a passage about a specific conflict with specific treaty-breakers, and the verses on either side say so.

Similarly, 2:191, "kill them wherever you overtake them", follows 2:190: "Fight in the way of God those who fight against you, but do not transgress. Indeed, God does not like transgressors." The passage continues with "if they cease, then there is to be no aggression except against the oppressors" (2:193). This site's rebuttals jihad and qital and Islam and terrorism work through these passages.

Layer two: the occasion of revelation

Many verses were revealed in response to a particular event, and the scholars collected reports of these occasions, called asbab al-nuzul. Knowing the occasion often clarifies what a verse addresses.

A clear example is 2:256, "there is no compulsion in religion". Abu Dawud reports from Ibn 'Abbas that before Islam, a woman of Medina whose children did not survive would sometimes vow that if a child lived she would raise it as a Jew. When the Jewish tribe of Banu al-Nadir were expelled, some of these children of the Ansar were among them, and their parents said: we will not leave our sons. Then the verse was revealed. Al-Albani graded the report sahih.1 The verse forbade the parents to compel their own children to return.

Occasions have limits as evidence. Reports about them vary in strength and should be graded like any hadith, as our guide hadith grading explained describes. And the scholars held a principle that a verse's meaning is taken from the generality of its wording, not only from the particular occasion. The occasion explains the verse; it does not always confine it.

Layer three: the whole Qur'an

The classical exegetes held that the Qur'an explains itself: a verse is read alongside other verses on the same subject. A reader who takes one verse on a subject and ignores the others has not read the Qur'an on that subject.

On fighting, for instance, the verses on war are read alongside verses on treaties, on protection, and on the sanctity of life: "whoever kills a soul, unless for a soul or for corruption in the land, it is as if he had slain mankind entirely" (5:32). On belief, 2:256 is read with 18:29, "whoever wills, let him believe; and whoever wills, let him disbelieve", and with 10:99, "would you compel the people in order that they become believers?"

Reading the Qur'an as a whole also raises the question of abrogation, naskh: the classical view that some later rulings replaced earlier ones. Scholars disagreed widely about how many verses this affects, and some modern scholars hold it applies to very few. This site's rebuttal abrogation and the edited book and the doubt verses that were cancelled discuss it, and the companion site has an article on Meccan and Medinan verses and abrogation.

Layer four: the Prophet's explanation

The Qur'an describes the Prophet as the one sent to "make clear to the people what was sent down to them" (16:44). The classical scholars therefore read verses alongside the Prophet's sayings and practice. On 4:34, which mentions striking a wife, they read the verse with the Prophet's Farewell Sermon, in which he said that if it came to that, the strike must not be severe, ghayr mubarrih (Muslim 1218).3 This does not settle every question about the verse, and our rebuttal Qur'an 4:34 in context and the doubt Qur'an 4:34 and wife-beating take the question seriously. But a reading that ignores the Prophet's explanation is not the reading the tradition gave.

Layer five: language

The Qur'an is in classical Arabic, and translations make choices. A single word can have several meanings, and translators choose one. The word muhaymin in 5:48, for example, is rendered "criterion", "guardian", "witness" or "trustee" in different translations, and the early exegetes recorded all of these.2 Our guide on the Islamic dilemma shows how much an argument can depend on one word. If a doubt turns on a single word, check more than one translation, and if you can, a classical dictionary or commentary.

Layer six: Mecca and Medina

The scholars divided the suras into Meccan and Medinan, revealed before and after the Prophet's emigration to Medina. The setting changed sharply between the two. In Mecca the Muslims were a small, persecuted group with no political power; the Meccan suras speak mostly of God, the Hereafter, the prophets and moral conduct. In Medina the Muslims formed a community with treaties, enemies, laws and wars, and the Medinan suras address all of these. A verse about fighting, treaties or punishment is almost always Medinan, and it was addressed to a community in a particular political situation.

This does not mean that Medinan verses are less binding, which is not the classical view. It means that a reader who wants to know what a Medinan verse required has to ask what situation it was addressing, who the parties were, and what had happened just before. The commentaries usually say.

Using a commentary

The classical commentaries, tafsir, collect the readings of the early generations on each verse. Those of al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi are among the most widely used, and the full Arabic texts are freely available online. English translations of Ibn Kathir's commentary exist in abridged form. A commentary will usually give you the occasion, the related verses and hadith, and the range of interpretations, often with the commentator's own preference. It is the quickest way to see that a verse you were told has "one obvious meaning" was read in several ways by the earliest Muslims.

What context does not do

It is important to be honest. Context explains; it does not always reassure. Some verses remain difficult when read carefully, and some readers, having read them carefully, still disagree with them. A guide that told you context would make every hard verse easy would be telling you something untrue. The aim of reading in context is not to arrive at a comfortable answer. It is to make sure that whatever you conclude about a verse, you have concluded it about the verse, and not about a sentence cut out of it.

Context is also not a tool for one side. Muslims sometimes quote verses out of context to reassure, just as critics do to alarm. "There is no compulsion in religion" quoted alone, without the rest of the passage or the classical debates about it, is no more honest than "kill them wherever you find them" quoted alone.

A method you can use

  1. Find the verse by its number and read at least five verses either side.
  2. Look up its occasion of revelation, and check how that report is graded.
  3. Find other verses on the same subject.
  4. Look for hadith in which the Prophet explained or applied it.
  5. Compare two or three translations, and note any key word.
  6. Read one classical commentary on the verse.
  7. Only then decide what you think.

If a verse troubles you, it is worth this effort. And if, after it, the verse still troubles you, you have a real question, which is worth more than a borrowed one. Our guide how to assess a doubt suggests what to do next.

title: Doubt and the Inner Life: al-Ghazali's al-Munqidh
excerpt: Al-Ghazali's al-Munqidh min al-Dalal: two months of radical doubt, a crisis that silenced him, and what his account offers a Muslim who doubts today.
body:
If you are a Muslim who doubts, you may feel that you are the first person to have felt this way, or that doubt is something the tradition has no room for. Neither is true. One of the most influential scholars in Islamic history, Abu Hamid al-Ghazali (d. 505 AH / 1111 CE), wrote an account of his own doubts, and it has been read for nine centuries. This guide introduces that account, al-Munqidh min al-Dalal, "The Deliverer from Error", and what it may offer a person who doubts today. It quotes al-Ghazali from the Arabic text and gives page links so that you can read him yourself.

Who al-Ghazali was

By his thirties al-Ghazali was the most celebrated scholar in Baghdad, a professor at the Nizamiyya college, a jurist, a theologian and a writer on philosophy. He wrote al-Munqidh late in life, when, as he says, he was past fifty, in reply to a friend who had asked him to describe how he had searched for truth among the competing schools of his day.1 It is short, personal, and unusually honest.

A thirst that was not chosen

Al-Ghazali says that from before the age of twenty he had plunged into every question, examining the beliefs of every group, and that the thirst to grasp the reality of things was "my habit and my way from the beginning of my affairs", an instinct God had placed in his nature "not by my choice or my contrivance".2

He describes the moment the bonds of inherited belief loosened. He noticed that the children of Christians grew up Christian, the children of Jews grew up Jewish, and the children of Muslims grew up Muslim. He recalled the hadith that every child is born upon the fitra, the original nature, and that it is the parents who make the child a Jew, a Christian or a Magian. And he wanted to know what that original nature was, beneath what parents and teachers had added.2

Many people who doubt today begin with exactly this observation. This site's doubt born into it and the rebuttal why this religion and not another take it up. What is striking is that al-Ghazali did not treat the question as an attack on faith. He treated it as the beginning of a search.

What he wanted: certainty

He decided that what he was looking for was certain knowledge, and he defined it strictly: knowledge in which the thing known is disclosed so completely that no doubt remains with it, and no possibility of error. His example is famous. If he knows that ten is more than three, and someone says "no, three is more, and as proof I will turn this stick into a snake", and does so, he would wonder at the man's power but would not doubt that ten is more than three.3

Measured against that standard, he found he had very little. He began to doubt even his senses: the eye sees a shadow standing still, but an hour later it has moved; it sees a star the size of a coin, yet geometry shows it larger than the earth. Then he asked whether reason itself might be judged by some higher faculty, as reason judges the senses, and he pointed to dreams, in which we believe things completely until we wake.4

Two months

He could not argue his way out. Every argument, he saw, would rest on the very first principles he was doubting. "The illness became difficult," he writes, "and lasted nearly two months, during which I was a sceptic in fact, though not in speech or statement". Then God cured him of that illness, and the necessary truths of reason returned, accepted and trusted, "not by arranging a proof or ordering an argument, but by a light that God cast into the breast, and that light is the key to most knowledge".5

He adds a sentence worth reading slowly: "whoever thinks that unveiling depends on carefully composed proofs has narrowed the vast mercy of God".5 He does not mean that arguments are useless; he spent the rest of the book on them. He means that a person does not hold on to reason by reason alone, and that the recovery of trust is a gift as much as an achievement.

The search through the schools

Recovered from radical scepticism, al-Ghazali examined the four groups of seekers of his time: the theologians, the Batinis who claimed an infallible teacher, the philosophers, and the Sufis. He studied each in depth, and wrote that he found theology adequate to its purpose, defending creed, but not to his purpose, which was certainty.6 His judgements on the others are detailed and sometimes severe; they are part of the history of Islamic thought, and readers still argue about them.

He also noted something about inherited belief that is useful for a doubter to hear. Once a person knows that he is merely imitating, he says, the glass of his imitation is broken, and it cannot be mended by patching; it must be melted down and made anew.7 In other words, there is no going back to the faith you had before you asked. If faith remains, it will be a different faith, one you have examined.

The second crisis

The book's most moving passage is about a second crisis, not of reason but of life. Al-Ghazali came to see that his teaching and his fame were bound up with a love of position, and he could not bring himself to leave them. For nearly six months, beginning in Rajab 488 AH, he says, he wavered between the pull of the world and the call of the Hereafter. Then "the matter passed from choice to compulsion": God locked his tongue so that he could not teach. He tried to teach even one day, for the sake of his students, and could not utter a single word.8

The paralysis of his tongue brought grief to his heart; he could not digest food, and his strength failed, until the physicians gave up hope, saying that this was something that had come down upon the heart and could not be treated by medicine.9 When he felt his helplessness completely, he turned to God "as one who is compelled, who has no way out", and God, he writes, made it easy for his heart to turn away from position, wealth, family and companions. He left Baghdad. He spent nearly two years in Syria in seclusion, and continued in this way, travelling and returning, for about ten years.10

What al-Ghazali offers a doubter now

You are not the first. A scholar whose works are still taught in every Muslim country doubted the reliability of his own senses and reason, and later suffered a collapse that the physicians of his time could not treat. He wrote about both without shame. The tradition kept his account and honoured it.

Doubt can be a stage, not an ending. Al-Ghazali's doubt was the beginning of a search, and he presents it as such. That is not a promise about where your search will lead; it is a description of where his did.

The heart matters. His second crisis was not about arguments at all. It was about what he loved and feared, and it showed itself in his body. Many people who doubt find, as he did, that the intellectual question and the inner one are tangled together. Our guide how to assess a doubt suggests ways of telling them apart, and the companion site's article did your heart leave before your head? looks at the same question.

Time is allowed. His first crisis took two months, his second six, and his recovery ten years. No one rushed him, and no one should rush you.

Inherited faith is not the only kind. The broken glass cannot be patched. If you come through your questions with faith, it will be faith you have tested. If you do not, you will at least know why.

Reading al-Munqidh critically

It would not be fair to present al-Ghazali as beyond criticism. His account was written years after the events and shaped by what he had come to believe. His judgements on the philosophers were contested in his own time and after, most famously by Ibn Rushd. And some of the reports he quotes as hadith are of uncertain strength; a book of personal testimony is not a hadith collection, and our guide hadith grading explained explains why that matters. None of this lessens the honesty of his account. It is a reason to read him as a fellow searcher rather than as an oracle.

If your doubt has become distress

Al-Ghazali's second crisis is a reminder that inner struggle can affect the body and the mind. If you are not sleeping, not eating, unable to work or study, or having thoughts of harming yourself, please treat that as a matter of health and talk to a doctor or counsellor, and if you are in danger, contact your local emergency number now. Our guide where to find support suggests where to begin. There is no merit in suffering alone, and nothing in the tradition requires it. The doubt doubting through Ramadan is written for one particular form of this experience, and the companion site's article your doubts are not a disease speaks to the shame many doubters feel.

title: Supporting Someone Who Doubts: For Families
excerpt: For families and friends of someone doubting Islam: keep them safe, listen before answering, respect their privacy, and keep the relationship.
body:
This guide is for parents, brothers and sisters, spouses and friends of someone who has told you, or shown you, that they are doubting Islam. It may be the hardest conversation your family has had. You may feel fear, grief, anger or shame, sometimes all at once. Those feelings are understandable. This guide is about what to do with them so that the person you love stays safe, stays close, and stays able to talk to you.

First: what doubt is, and what it is not

Doubt is not apostasy. In no school of Islamic law is a person who has questions, who struggles to pray, or who reads criticism, an apostate. The Prophet's Companions told him that they found thoughts in themselves too terrible to speak, and he told them that this was clear faith (Muslim 132).1 Some of the greatest scholars in Islamic history wrote openly about their doubts; our guide doubt and the inner life tells the story of one of them.

Doubt is also not usually a rebellion against you. People doubt for many reasons: an argument they met online, a verse or hadith they cannot reconcile, a painful experience, a sense of not belonging, depression, or simply growing up and asking questions for the first time. Our guide how to assess a doubt describes the different kinds. Very often the person is as frightened as you are.

Safety comes before everything else

Before any conversation about belief, make sure the person is safe. That means safe from violence, from threats, from being forced out of the home with nowhere to go, and from harm to themselves.

Be honest with yourself about your own household and community. If anyone in your family or circle might react with violence, threats, forced marriage, confinement, or by taking away the person's documents, money or phone, the first duty is to prevent that. None of these is permitted. Even the classical law of apostasy, which our guide what apostasy is in Islamic law describes, gave no individual the right to harm anyone, and the classical jurists condemned anyone who took the law into his own hands.2 Shaming, beating or threatening a person into belief is also pointless on Islam's own terms: "there is no compulsion in religion" (2:256), and faith produced by fear is not faith.

If you are worried that the person may harm themselves, take it seriously. Ask them directly and calmly whether they have thought about it. Asking does not put the idea in their head. If the answer is yes, or you are not sure, help them contact a doctor or a crisis line, and in an emergency call your local emergency number.

Listen before you answer

The most common mistake families make is to answer before they have listened. A person who tells you they are doubting has taken a risk. If the first thing they hear is an argument, a lecture or tears, they learn that it is not safe to talk to you, and they stop.

Try instead to ask, and to keep asking. What is troubling you? When did it start? Is it a particular question, or something more general? How are you feeling? Listen to the answers without interrupting. You do not need to agree with what you hear. You need to understand it.

Some things are better not said, at least at first:

  • "You have been brainwashed" or "Who has been talking to you?" These suggest the person cannot think for themselves.
  • "You are going to Hell." Whatever you believe about the Hereafter, a threat ends the conversation. The Prophet was sent as a reminder, not a controller (88:21-22).
  • "What will people say?" This tells the person that your reputation matters more than they do.
  • "You were never a real Muslim." This is unkind, and usually untrue.

Do not make yourself the opponent

If you turn every conversation into a debate, you become the opposing side, and the person's doubts become a position to defend. That makes it harder, not easier, for them to change their mind if they ever want to.

If they ask you a question you cannot answer, say so. "I do not know, but I would like to find out with you" is a better answer than a bad argument. You can suggest resources, such as this site's doubts and rebuttals, or a knowledgeable scholar who is known for listening. But offer them; do not impose them. And be careful whom you recommend. A scholar who shouts or shames will do more harm than none.

Keep the relationship

Whatever happens with their beliefs, keep the relationship. Eat together. Talk about other things. Invite them to family occasions. Let them know, in words and actions, that they are still your child, your sibling, your friend. A person who feels loved and safe is able to think clearly; a person who feels rejected is driven towards whoever will accept them.

The Qur'an is clear that kindness to parents does not depend on their beliefs: even parents who strive to make their child associate others with God are to be accompanied in this world "with kindness" (31:15). If that is owed to parents who pressure a child towards disbelief, a family can surely show kindness to a child who has questions.

Many people who leave describe loneliness as the hardest part: the loss not of a belief but of a family and a world. This site's doubts leaving would cost me my family and alone on the other side are written for them. The companion site's article the social cost of leaving describes the same thing from outside. You can make sure your family is not part of that cost.

When the person is young

If the person doubting is a teenager living at home, the balance of power is very unequal, and that makes your restraint more important, not less. Young people often test ideas aloud, sometimes provocatively, as part of working out who they are. Many will settle their questions in their own time if they are allowed to ask them. Punishment, confiscating a phone, or cutting a child off from friends for asking about religion tends to drive the questions underground, where you cannot help with them. Keep the conversation open, keep their routine stable, and keep an eye on their wellbeing: sleep, school, mood. If you see signs of depression or self-harm, involve a doctor.

Respect their privacy

Do not tell others about the person's doubts without their permission: not the extended family, not the mosque, not their school or employer. In some places and some communities, being known as a doubter or as someone who has left can carry real social and legal risks. Our guide leaving and the law sets out where. The person's story is theirs to tell, if and when they choose.

The same applies online. Do not post about them, and do not search their phone or accounts. Trust broken in this way is very hard to rebuild.

Look after yourself too

You may be grieving. You may be afraid for the person's future, or their Hereafter. You may feel you have failed as a parent. These feelings are real, and you deserve support with them. Talk to someone you trust who will keep the matter private, or to a counsellor. If you pray, pray. The Qur'an tells of Nuh pleading for his son (11:45) and of Ibrahim speaking gently to his father, "peace be upon you" (19:47). Neither was followed by the one he loved, and the Qur'an's rule is that "no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another" (6:164). A parent's love and prayer are not wasted, and a child's choice is not a parent's sin.

And remember that the story is not over. People's beliefs change over years, in every direction. Some who doubt come through their questions with a stronger faith; some leave; some come back after many years. Our guide coming back is about return. What you can control is whether your home is somewhere the person can always come back to.

If they have already decided to leave

If the person tells you they no longer believe, the advice above still applies: safety, listening, privacy, and keeping the relationship. You do not have to agree with their decision, and you do not have to pretend that it does not hurt. But you do have to treat them with dignity. There is no school of Islamic law that permits a family to harm, imprison or disown a person into belief, and no ruling that obliges you to cut them off.

Practical matters may follow, about marriage, inheritance or documents, depending on the law where you live. Get accurate information rather than relying on rumour, and do not use these matters as leverage.

What you can say

If you do not know what to say, here are some words you might use, in your own way:

  • "Thank you for telling me. I know that was hard."
  • "I love you. That does not change."
  • "I do not understand all of this yet, but I want to."
  • "You are safe here."
  • "Take your time. We can talk whenever you want."

None of these requires you to give up your own faith or to pretend to agree. They only require you to put the person first. That is not a weakness of faith. It is mercy, which the tradition places at the centre of everything.

If there is danger now

If the person you are worried about is in danger from someone, or from themselves, contact your local emergency number now. Our guide where to find support lists other kinds of help.
