Ibn Qudama, al-Mughni (Maktabat al-Qahira ed.), Kitab al-Murtadd: killing or harming an apostate without the ruler is wrong and punishable.

title: Where to Find Support
excerpt: Where to find help when doubt or leaving has become hard: safety first, mental health, someone to talk to, legal help, and how to tell if help is safe.
body:
This guide is about finding help when you are struggling with faith, with doubt, or with what has happened since you began to question. It does not recommend particular organisations, because this site cannot check every group's practices in every country, and a recommendation that turned out to be wrong could put you at risk. Instead it explains the kinds of help that exist, how to find them where you live, and how to tell whether a source of help is safe.

If you are in danger right now, from another person or from yourself, stop reading and contact your local emergency number. In most of Europe that is 112; in the United Kingdom 999; in the United States and Canada 911. If you do not know the number where you are, a search for "emergency number" and the name of your country will give it.

Know what kind of help you need

"Support" covers very different needs. It helps to name yours, because each is met in a different place.

  • Immediate safety: you are being threatened, hurt, confined, or pressured into marriage, or you fear that you will be.
  • Mental health: you are anxious, depressed, not sleeping, unable to function, or having thoughts of harming yourself.
  • Someone to talk to: you need to speak about your questions with a person who will listen and not judge.
  • Answers: you want to look into your questions with someone knowledgeable.
  • Practical and legal help: you have questions about housing, documents, marriage, custody or your legal position.
  • Community: you feel alone and want to meet others who have been through similar questions.

You may need more than one. Start with whichever is most urgent, and safety always comes first.

Immediate safety

If you are at risk of violence, of being forced into marriage, or of being taken abroad against your will, contact the police through the emergency number. In many countries the police and social services have specialist units for family violence, forced marriage and so-called honour-based abuse. Your local police non-emergency line, a domestic violence helpline, or a government website for your country can tell you what exists.

Think about your safety before you make any disclosure. If telling your family that you doubt might put you in danger, you do not have to tell them, and you do not have to tell them now. Keep a copy of your important documents, such as passport and identity card, somewhere safe, and if you can, keep some money and a phone that others cannot take from you. Keep a note of a few people you trust and their numbers.

Be careful with your devices. If others can see your phone, browser history or accounts, consider using a private browsing window, logging out of shared devices, and changing passwords. Many domestic violence services publish guidance on staying safe online.

Mental health

Questions about faith can be deeply distressing, and distress is a health matter. A general practitioner or family doctor is often the best first step; they can refer you to counselling or other treatment. Many universities and colleges have free and confidential counselling services, and many employers offer confidential support schemes.

If you are having thoughts of suicide or self-harm, please contact a crisis line or emergency services now. Most countries have a free, confidential crisis line available at any hour. Your doctor, a hospital, or a search for "crisis line" and the name of your country will find it. If you are outside your home country, the emergency number where you are will connect you to help.

When you look for a therapist or counsellor, it is reasonable to ask how they approach religious questions. A good therapist will not try to push you towards belief or away from it. You can ask directly: "Will you respect whatever I decide about my faith?" Our guide how to assess a doubt explains that some intrusive, repetitive religious thoughts are a recognised feature of anxiety and obsessive-compulsive disorder, and respond to treatment; a clinician can help you tell the difference.

Someone to talk to

Sometimes the most important help is a person who will listen. That might be a friend, a relative, a teacher, a counsellor, or a religious figure you trust. What matters is that they are safe: that they will keep what you tell them private, will not shame you, and will not report you to anyone.

Before confiding in someone, it is reasonable to test the water. Mention a question in general terms and see how they react. If they respond with anger or alarm, they may not be the right person yet.

This site's doubts section exists partly for this purpose: each entry is written for a person carrying a particular question, and you can read them privately. If your situation is about family, leaving would cost me my family and afraid of what happens if I leave may help. If you have already left and feel isolated, alone on the other side is written for you.

Answers

If what you need is to look into your questions, find a scholar or teacher known for patience and honesty, who will take your question seriously and admit what they do not know. Avoid anyone who answers questions with threats or insults. Read widely, including the classical sources, which are freely available. This site's rebuttals and guides, and the companion site's articles, such as is doubt permitted in Islam?, are a place to start. Our guides hadith grading explained and reading the Qur'an in context explain how to check sources for yourself.

Practical and legal help

Questions about marriage, divorce, custody, inheritance or official documents depend entirely on the law of the country where you live, and sometimes on which court has jurisdiction over you. Get advice from a qualified lawyer in your country. Many countries have free or low-cost legal advice services, law school clinics, or legal aid. Our guide leaving and the law gives an overview by region, but it is not legal advice.

If you are at risk and considering leaving your country, seek advice before you travel. Asylum and refugee law is complicated, and decisions made in a hurry can be hard to undo.

Community

Many people who doubt find it helps to meet others who have asked the same questions. There are groups for questioning Muslims, for people who have left Islam, and for people who have returned to it, both in person and online. This site does not list them, because it cannot vouch for each one. When you consider a group, ask these questions.

  • Does it protect members' privacy? Does it allow pseudonyms, and does it keep membership confidential?
  • Does it let people reach their own conclusions, or does it push them in one direction?
  • Is it open about who runs it and how it is funded?
  • Does it encourage you to keep your relationships, or to cut people off?
  • Does it treat people who disagree with respect?

A group that pressures you, demands secrecy about itself while exposing you, or tells you to cut off everyone who disagrees, is not safe, whichever direction it pushes. The companion site's article how Muslims leave: the sociology discusses some patterns in these communities, and this site's rebuttal what the testimonies actually do discusses online testimony.

If you are a student or living away from home

Students are often in a particular position: living away from family for the first time, meeting new ideas, and sometimes financially dependent on parents who may react badly. If that is you, your institution's student services are a good place to start. Most universities have confidential counselling, welfare advisers, and staff trained to help students facing family pressure, including pressure about marriage. They can also advise on emergency funds and accommodation if your situation at home changes. You do not need to explain your beliefs to ask for help; it is enough to say that you are under pressure and need advice.

If you are under eighteen, the situation is different again. A school counsellor, a teacher you trust, or a children's helpline in your country can help, and they have duties to keep children safe. You do not have to have decided anything about your faith to ask them for help.

Signs a source of help is not safe

  • It asks for money before helping you, or promises outcomes it cannot guarantee.
  • It asks you to share private information publicly, or to identify your family.
  • It shames you for your questions, in either direction.
  • It discourages you from seeing a doctor or a lawyer.
  • It cannot or will not tell you who is behind it.

For families and friends

If you are reading this because someone you love is doubting, our guide supporting someone who doubts is written for you. The most important help you can give is to make sure they are safe, and to remain someone they can talk to.

A final word

Asking for help is not weakness, and it is not betrayal of anyone. Whatever you are going through, you deserve safety, privacy and time. If nothing else in this guide helps today, remember the first instruction: if you are in danger, contact your local emergency number.

title: Leaving Islam and the Law, Region by Region
excerpt: How the law treats leaving Islam around the world, with statutes cited: criminal penalties, blasphemy laws and personal status consequences.
body:
This guide summarises how the law treats leaving Islam in different parts of the world, citing the statutes where they exist. It describes law; it advocates nothing; and it is not legal advice. Laws change, courts interpret them differently, and the practical situation is often shaped as much by family and community as by any statute. If your own position matters to you, take advice from a qualified lawyer in your country, and keep your safety first.

One point before the detail. Doubting is not a crime anywhere. No statute in any country criminalises having questions, reading, or being unsure. The provisions below concern formal renunciation, public expression, or the civil consequences of a recorded change of religion.

Three kinds of legal consequence

It helps to separate three things that are often confused.

Criminal penalties for apostasy itself. A small number of states treat leaving Islam as a crime, either in a written penal code or through courts applying uncodified classical law.

Laws on blasphemy, insulting religion and proselytism. Many more states have no apostasy offence, but criminalise insulting religion, "shaking the faith" of a Muslim, or distributing material against Islam. A person who leaves quietly may never meet these laws; a person who speaks publicly may.

Civil and personal status consequences. In many states, family matters are governed by religious personal status law. Leaving Islam can affect marriage, custody, inheritance and the religion recorded on identity documents, even where it is no crime. For many people this is where the law actually bites.

This site's rebuttal apostasy and the classical law and the guide the apostasy penalty explain where the classical rulings came from. This guide is about the law as it stands.

International law

The Universal Declaration of Human Rights, article 18, states that everyone has the right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion, including "freedom to change his religion or belief". The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, article 18, protects freedom "to have or to adopt a religion or belief of his choice" and forbids coercion that would impair it. The UN Human Rights Committee's General Comment No. 22 (1993) states that this includes the right to replace one's religion with another or to adopt atheistic views. Most Muslim-majority states are parties to the Covenant, some with reservations. The companion site's article apostasy and international law discusses this further.

The Gulf and the Arabian Peninsula

Saudi Arabia has no codified penal code for hudud offences; courts apply classical Islamic law directly, under which apostasy is a capital offence in principle. Prosecutions are often brought under other headings, such as laws on terrorism or cybercrime.

Yemen's Republican Decree Law No. 12 of 1994 on Crimes and Penalties, article 259, provides the death penalty for apostasy after an invitation to repent.

Qatar's Penal Code (Law No. 11 of 2004), article 1, applies the Islamic law provisions on hudud, including apostasy, to Muslims. The United Arab Emirates and Kuwait have no codified apostasy offence in their main penal codes, but apply personal status consequences, and their laws on insulting religion are broad.

The Levant and Iraq

Jordan, Iraq, Syria and Lebanon have no criminal offence of apostasy in their penal codes. In each, family matters for Muslims fall under religious personal status law and courts, and a recorded change of religion can affect the validity of a marriage, custody of children and inheritance. Iraq's Personal Status Law No. 188 of 1959 governs Muslims' family matters. Lebanon's system is confessional: each recognised community has its own personal status courts, and since 2009 citizens have been able to have their sect removed from the civil register, though marriage still largely depends on religious institutions.

Iran and Afghanistan

Iran's Islamic Penal Code of 2013 does not list apostasy among its defined offences, but article 220 directs judges to apply authoritative Islamic sources for hudud not mentioned in the code, in accordance with article 167 of the Constitution. Courts have used this route.

Afghanistan, under the Taliban since 2021, applies its own interpretation of Hanafi law without a published penal code for these offences.

Africa

Mauritania's Penal Code, article 306, provides for apostasy and blasphemy; a 2018 amendment made the death penalty mandatory for blasphemy and removed the possibility of avoiding it by repentance for that offence.

Sudan repealed article 126 of its Criminal Act 1991, which had made apostasy a capital crime, by the Miscellaneous Amendments (Fundamental Rights and Freedoms) Act of July 2020. The situation since the outbreak of war in 2023 is unclear.

Egypt has no apostasy offence. Article 98(f) of the Penal Code penalises "contempt of religion", and personal status consequences are significant: in the Nasr Hamid Abu Zayd case, the Court of Cassation in 1996 upheld the separation of a professor from his wife on the ground of apostasy. Religion is recorded on the national identity card.

Morocco's Penal Code, article 220, penalises using inducements to "shake the faith" of a Muslim or convert him. Algeria's Ordinance 06-03 of 2006 regulates non-Muslim worship and penalises inciting a Muslim to convert. Tunisia's Constitution of 2022 guarantees freedom of belief and conscience, as its 2014 Constitution did.

South Asia

Pakistan has no apostasy offence. Its blasphemy provisions, sections 295-B and 295-C of the Penal Code, are among the most severe in the world, section 295-C carrying the death penalty for defiling the name of the Prophet, and accusations can lead to mob violence regardless of the outcome in court. Bangladesh and India have no apostasy offence; India's personal laws can affect marriage and inheritance on conversion.

Southeast Asia

Brunei's Syariah Penal Code Order 2013, section 112, provides for apostasy, with the heaviest penalties applicable on certain standards of proof. Brunei announced a moratorium on the death penalty in 2019.

Malaysia has no federal apostasy offence. Article 11 of the Federal Constitution protects freedom of religion, but article 121(1A) excludes the civil courts from matters within the jurisdiction of the Syariah courts, and in Lina Joy v Majlis Agama Islam Wilayah Persekutuan (2007) the Federal Court held that a Muslim's change of religion is for the Syariah courts. Several state enactments penalise attempts to leave Islam or provide for detention for rehabilitation. This site's rebuttal religion by registration discusses the registration side.

Indonesia has no apostasy offence. Its blasphemy law, Presidential Decree No. 1/PNPS/1965, remains in force, and the new Criminal Code (Law No. 1 of 2023), due to take effect in 2026, carries offences relating to religion. Religion is recorded on the identity card, with a limited list of options.

Turkey, Central Asia and the Balkans

Turkey, the Central Asian republics and the Muslim-majority states of the Balkans have secular legal systems with no apostasy offence. Social and family consequences may still be real.

Europe, North America and elsewhere

Leaving any religion is lawful throughout Europe, North America, Australia and most of the world. Article 9 of the European Convention on Human Rights protects the freedom to change religion. In these countries the risks, where they exist, come from family or community pressure, not from the state, and the law offers protection against them: against threats, violence, forced marriage and coercive control. If you face any of these, the police are there to protect you.

Children, marriage and inheritance

Across many systems that apply religious personal status law, three civil questions recur. A marriage between a Muslim woman and a non-Muslim man is generally not recognised, and a recorded change of religion by one spouse can be treated as ending the marriage. Custody decisions may weigh the religion of each parent. And classical inheritance rules exclude inheritance between a Muslim and a non-Muslim, so a person who leaves may be excluded from a parent's estate. How these rules apply depends on the specific code and court, and some states have reformed them. If any of them affects you, take specific legal advice before acting.

What this means in practice

In most of the world, no court will ever be interested in what you believe. The real risks for most people who doubt or leave are social: family reaction, community pressure, employment, and, in some places, the effect on marriage and children. Those risks can be serious. They are also risks you can plan for. Our guides where to find support and supporting someone who doubts may help, and this site's rebuttal what leaving actually costs and the companion site's article on the scale of leaving describe the wider picture.

If you are in a country where the law itself is a danger, be careful about what you say publicly and online, and about what you put in writing. Do not change official records or make public declarations without legal advice. If you are in immediate danger, contact your local emergency number.

A caution on this guide

Every entry above is a summary, and laws change. Some provisions are rarely enforced and others are enforced in ways the text does not suggest. Before relying on anything here, check the current law with a qualified lawyer in the country concerned.

title: Coming Back: Tawbah After Leaving
excerpt: For anyone thinking of returning to Islam: what the Qur'an and the Prophet said about tawbah, what return involves, and answers to the most common fears.
body:
This guide is for a person who has drifted from Islam, or left it, and is thinking about coming back. It may also help someone who never formally left but feels too far away to return. It explains what the Qur'an and the Prophet said about tawbah, turning back to God, and answers the fears people most often have. It is written gently, because returning is hard enough without anyone making it harder.

The word

Tawbah comes from a root meaning to return. The same word is used for the person turning back to God and for God turning towards the person: one of God's names in the Qur'an is al-Tawwab, the One who returns again and again to those who return. Return is not a transaction in which a person earns readmission. It is a meeting, in which God is described as turning first.

Is the door really open?

Many people who think of returning have been told, or have read, that it is too late: that someone who has left can never be forgiven. The verses usually quoted are 3:86, which asks how God should guide a people who disbelieved after believing, and 4:137, about those who believed, then disbelieved, then believed, then disbelieved, then increased in disbelief.

Read the passage in 3:86-90 to its end. After the warning comes this: "except for those who repent after that and correct themselves; for indeed God is Forgiving and Merciful" (3:89). The exception is part of the same passage, and it describes exactly the person who comes back. The verse that follows, 3:90, speaks of those who "increase in disbelief", and 4:137 likewise ends with "then increased in disbelief": both describe people who continue, not people who return. If 3:89 is to mean anything, the person who returns is not shut out. This site's rebuttal return after leaving works through these verses in detail.

The general promise of the Qur'an is wider still: "Say, O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of God. Indeed, God forgives all sins. Indeed, it is He who is the Forgiving, the Merciful" (39:53). And of those who repent, believe and do good: "for them God will replace their evil deeds with good" (25:70).

What the Prophet said

The Prophet described God's joy at a servant's return with an image: God is more pleased with the repentance of His servant than one of you who lost his camel in a desert and then found it (al-Bukhari 6309).1 The image is of relief and gladness, not reluctant permission.

When 'Amr ibn al-'As came to accept Islam and hesitated, asking for his past to be forgiven, the Prophet told him that Islam wipes out what came before it (Muslim 121).2 And he said that God accepts the repentance of His servant until the death rattle (al-Tirmidhi 3537, graded hasan gharib by al-Tirmidhi).3 In other words, while a person lives, it is not too late.

What returning involves

The scholars described repentance simply. Al-Nawawi, at the start of the chapter on repentance in Riyad al-Salihin, records the scholars' statement that repentance from a sin between a servant and God has three conditions: to stop the sin, to regret it, and to resolve never to return to it. Where a sin involves another person's rights, there is a fourth: to put right what was taken, or seek their pardon.4

For a person who left Islam and wishes to return, the classical jurists held that one re-enters Islam by the testimony of faith: bearing witness that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is His Messenger. Ibn Qudama, in al-Mughni, discusses how a person's entry into Islam is established, and reports the view that even saying "I am a Muslim" can suffice, because it expresses what the testimony contains.5 No ceremony is required, no witnesses, no payment, and no one's permission.

You may wish to say the testimony with a trusted friend or at a mosque, and some people find a fresh start helped by a bath of purification and a first prayer. But the heart of return is between you and God. You can do it alone, today, in your own words.

Common fears

"I have left before and come back before. Surely this time it is too late." The Prophet's words above set no limit while a person lives. A person who returns many times is still returning. Our doubt can I come back? speaks to this fear directly.

"I still have doubts." Returning does not require that every question be answered. Many believers live with unanswered questions all their lives. The Prophet told Companions troubled by thoughts they could hardly speak that this was clear faith (Muslim 132). Our guides how to assess a doubt and doubt and the inner life may help you carry them.

"I did things while I was away that I am ashamed of." "Islam wipes out what came before it." The Qur'an promises that for those who repent, evil deeds are replaced with good (25:70). Shame can be a sign of a living conscience; it should not become a wall.

"I cannot pray five times a day yet." Start where you are. Pray what you can, and build. The Qur'an says that God does not burden a soul beyond its capacity (2:286). A person who prays one prayer sincerely has done more than one who waits for a perfect beginning that never comes.

"I am afraid of how my family or community will react." Some families will rejoice; some may be suspicious, or ask questions you are not ready to answer. Their reaction is not a ruling. Nothing in the sources lets a community refuse a person God has said He accepts. You do not owe anyone a public account of where you have been.

"I am afraid of the law." In the classical law, the jurists required that a person who left be invited to return, and 'Umar's reported words about such a person were "perhaps he will repent".6 Return was the outcome the law hoped for. In practice, in almost every country, returning to Islam carries no legal risk at all.

Returning to a community

Return to God and return to a community are not the same thing, and the second can be harder. You may need to find a mosque or circle where you feel welcome, and that may not be the one you left. Look for people who are kind, who do not pry, and who will let you grow at your own pace. If you were hurt by a community, it is reasonable to look elsewhere. The doubt I was hurt and nobody helped and the rebuttal where was God when I was hurt are written for those who left after harm.

The companion site's article coming back after leaving walks through return at more length, and this site's finite sins and the fire addresses a related fear about judgement.

Sincere repentance

The Qur'an calls believers to "repent to God with sincere repentance" (66:8), tawbatan nasuha. Sincerity does not mean perfection. It means that the return is real: that you mean it now, as much as you can mean anything. If you fall again, you return again. The tradition has never asked more than that.

The Qur'an also describes the repentance God accepts as that of "those who do wrong in ignorance and then repent soon after" (4:17). Ibn Kathir, commenting on the verse, reports Mujahid and others as saying that everyone who disobeys God, by mistake or deliberately, is "ignorant" until he leaves the sin, and reports Qatada's account that the Companions agreed that every sin is done in ignorance, deliberate or not. He explains "soon" as any time before the soul is taken, before the death rattle.7 That reading is generous, and the early generations meant it to be. Whatever your past, the verse that seems to narrow the door turns out, in their reading, to hold it open.

If returning feels impossible right now

You may want to come back and find that you cannot yet, because of what you feel, what you believe, or what is happening around you. That is not failure. Wanting to return is itself a turning. Take your time. Read, pray if you can, talk to someone kind.

And if you are struggling with your mental health, with guilt that will not lift, or with thoughts of harming yourself, please look after that first. Talk to a doctor or a counsellor, and if you are in danger, contact your local emergency number. Our guide where to find support suggests where to start. God's mercy does not depend on your being well enough to deserve it, and getting help is not a detour from return.

In short

  • The door is open while you live (3:89; 39:53; al-Tirmidhi 3537).
  • Return is by sincere turning, and for one who left, by the testimony of faith. No ceremony, witness or permission is required.
  • Past wrongs are wiped out and replaced with good (Muslim 121; 25:70).
  • Doubts, shame and imperfect practice do not bar return.
  • A community's reaction is not God's judgement.

title: Is Islam False? A Fair Guide for Doubters
excerpt: Is Islam false, or fake? A calm, fair guide for doubters: what the question asks, a short map of each angle, and where to read the full case on each.
seo_title: Is Islam False? A Fair Guide for Doubters
body:
If you have typed "is Islam false" into a search bar late at night, or "is Islam fake", or "why Islam is false", this guide is for you. You are not the first person to ask, and asking is not a crime against yourself or against God. This page does not try to win an argument in five minutes. It frames the question of whether Islam is false so that it can be looked at fairly, gives a short summary of each of the main angles, and sends you to the longer pages on this site, and to the evidence article on Compelling Evidence, where each angle is treated properly.

One thing first. Feeling that Islam might be false, or being frightened by the thought, is not a sign that something is wrong with you. The Prophet's Companions told him they found thoughts in themselves they could hardly bring themselves to speak, and he told them that this was clear faith (Muslim 132). The discomfort itself was not held against them. A question that frightens you is still a question, and it can be looked at calmly.

If the question has come with distress you cannot carry, if you are not sleeping, if you are thinking of harming yourself, or if you are afraid of someone at home, please put this page down and go to Where to Find Support first. In an emergency, call your local emergency number. In Malaysia, Befrienders KL is on 03-7627 2929 and the Talian Kasih line is 15999. Elsewhere, findahelpline.com lists free, confidential lines by country. The argument will still be here tomorrow.

Is Islam false? What the question is really asking

"Is Islam false?" sounds like one question. It is usually several, folded together. Some people mean: is there a God at all? Some mean: granted a God, did He speak through Muhammad, peace be upon him? Some mean: is the Qur'an we hold the book he brought? Some mean: are the hadith reliable? And many people, if they are honest, mean something else: why did the Muslims around me treat me the way they did, and does that show the religion is fake?

These are different questions with different kinds of evidence. A strong point about one of them does not settle the others. A weak answer you once heard from a teacher does not settle any of them. The first and most useful step is the one set out in How to Assess a Doubt: write your doubt down in one sentence. "Islam is false because..." Finish the sentence. You may find you have one reason, or three, or a feeling with no reason yet. All of those are honest places to stand, and each points to a different page below.

The Qur'an itself invites this. It does not ask to be believed without looking. "Produce your proof, if you should be truthful" (2:111) is said to those who make a claim without one, and the same standard is a fair one to hold Islam to. It tells the reader not to pursue "that of which you have no knowledge" (17:36), and it asks, "Then do they not reflect upon the Qur'an? If it had been from [any] other than Allah, they would have found within it much contradiction" (4:82). A tradition that sets a test of its own does not need you to stop asking.

Why people conclude Islam is false: the main angles

What follows is a map, not a verdict. Each angle gets a short, fair summary of the objection and of the Muslim answer, and a link to the page on this site that owns it. Those pages are long for a reason, and this guide does not repeat them.

"I was only Muslim because I was born into it"

This is perhaps the most common reason people give for thinking Islam is fake: had I been born in another house, I would hold another faith with the same confidence. The observation is true, and the tradition said it first. The Prophet said every child is born upon the fitra, and his parents make him a Jew, a Christian or a Magian (al-Bukhari 1385). The Qur'an condemns religion held only because one's fathers held it (2:170). The question is whether the observation shows a belief is false, or only that it has not yet been examined. That inference is tested in Why this religion and not another, and the lived side of it, the feeling of never having chosen, is taken up in Born into it and I was never asked.

"The Qur'an contradicts the Bible it confirms"

A popular argument from Christian apologists says the Qur'an praises the Torah and Gospel, which contradict it, so Islam is false either way. This has its own long guide, The Islamic Dilemma: A Fair Guide for Doubters, which sets out the argument at its strongest, the classical answers, and the limits of both. Read it there rather than in summary here.

"The miracles argument fell apart"

Many people were taught that the Qur'an predicted modern science, then found the claims stretched. When that collapses, it can feel as if Islam itself was the stretch. But the scientific-miracles genre is recent, and the Qur'an never rested its case on it. The difference between a weak argument for Islam and a strong argument against Islam is set out in The scientific miracles genre and, from the reader's side, The miracles argument. The Qur'an's own challenge, the one it does make, is in The challenge.

"The hadith are unreliable, so everything is"

Some readers find a hadith that shocks them, or learn the collections were compiled generations after the Prophet, and conclude that the whole edifice is fake. The tradition graded its reports and rejected many; a weak or forged report is not part of the religion. How grading works is in Hadith Grading Explained for Doubters; the gap in time is in The two-centuries gap; and the pattern of moving from one troubling report to rejecting everything is examined in The slide from hadith to nothing.

"The moral teachings are wrong"

For many, the reason Islam seems false is moral: a verse on women, on war, on slavery, on apostasy. These are serious questions and they deserve their own pages, not a paragraph. Start with Reading the Qur'an in Context, then the specific entry, for example Qur'an 4:34 in context or Captives and slavery. On the apostasy penalty, which frightens many readers for personal reasons, see The Apostasy Penalty: Evidence and Debate.

"If God is real, why so much suffering?"

The problem of evil is not a problem for Islam alone, but it is often the question underneath "is Islam false". Fairness means facing that it is a question about God before it is a question about any one religion. See The argument from evil, and, if the question comes from a loss or a hurt of your own, Why so much suffering and Doubts after a death.

"Muslims cannot even agree, and the ummah is broken"

Disagreement between Muslims, and the state of Muslim societies, lead many to ask why Islam is false if it is meant to guide. These are arguments about people, and they are real, but they are a different kind of evidence from arguments about whether the message is true. See Sects and division and The state of the Muslims.

"I was hurt by Muslims"

Sometimes the reason a person thinks Islam is fake has nothing to do with texts. It is a teacher who humiliated them, a family that used religion as a weapon, a community that looked away. That pain is real and it is not your fault. It is also worth knowing that your hurt and the truth of Islam are two separate questions, and that you are allowed to deal with the first before the second. See I was hurt and nobody helped and Hurt by a religious teacher.

"Everything I read online says Islam is false"

If your doubts grew in one feed, it is worth asking what the feed was built to do. Polemical channels on every side select the strongest-sounding clips and rarely show the reply. That does not make them wrong, but it does mean you have heard one side. See The echo chamber and The websites.

The case that Islam is not false

A fair guide should not only list objections. The positive case for Islam, the preservation of the Qur'an, the life of the Prophet, the coherence of its account of God, and the argument from the Qur'an's own challenge, is made at length on our sister site. Read Is Islam false? The evidence, on Compelling Evidence. It is written for the same question you are asking, and it states its evidence so that you can check it. This site's job is different: to sit with the doubt; that site's job is to set out the case. Reading both is the fairest thing you can do.

How to weigh whether Islam is false, without rushing

A few principles, offered gently, for working through the question honestly.

Separate the questions. Is there a God? Did He send Muhammad? Is the Qur'an his? Are this particular hadith or ruling sound? A no to the last does not give a no to the first.

Read the strongest form of both sides. If you have only read why Islam is false, read the best Muslim answer. If you have only heard the Muslim answer, read the strongest objection. Ask whether each side is answering what the other actually said.

Notice the source. A claim from a debate clip, a sermon, or a forum is a starting point, not a conclusion. Check the verse against a full translation and its context, and check the hadith and its grading.

Give it time. Big questions are rarely settled in a week. You do not owe anyone a decision tonight, not your family, not a stranger online, and not this site. The inner side of that slow work is the subject of Doubt and the Inner Life, which follows al-Ghazali through his own crisis of certainty.

Talk to someone safe. A knowledgeable, patient person who will not shame you is worth more than a hundred videos. If there is no such person around you, that is common, and it is not your failing. Families who want to help can read Supporting Someone Who Doubts.

If you have already decided Islam is false

Some readers arrive here having already concluded. This site will not threaten you. The Qur'an says, "There shall be no compulsion in [acceptance of] the religion" (2:256), and we take that seriously. If you are thinking about what leaving would mean in practice, there are legal and personal risks that depend on where you live, and you should know them before you speak openly. See Leaving Islam and the Law, Region by Region, What leaving costs, and The fear itself. Please do not put yourself in danger to prove a point. Your safety comes first.

And if, one day, you want to look again, the door does not close. The Qur'an says, "Do not despair of the mercy of Allah. Indeed, Allah forgives all sins" (39:53). See Coming Back: Tawbah After Leaving.

Common questions about whether Islam is false

Is it a sin to ask whether Islam is false? Asking is not the same as rejecting. The Companions were troubled by thoughts they could hardly speak of, and the Prophet called their distress at those thoughts clear faith (Muslim 132). The Qur'an repeatedly asks its readers to reflect, and praises "those of understanding" who look at the signs in creation (3:190).

Is Islam fake if so many scholars disagree? Disagreement among scholars is mostly about law and detail, and the tradition recorded it openly. It is evidence that people argued carefully, not that the core is invented. Whether the core is true is the question the evidence article addresses.

Why do some smart people say Islam is false? Intelligent people hold every position on religion. That tells you the question is hard, not which answer is right. The question is always which reasons are good, which is why this guide sends you to the reasons.

What if I cannot decide? Then you have not decided, and that is allowed. Many people live honestly with an open question for a long time. Keep reading, keep asking, and look after yourself while you do.

Who can I talk to? If you need to talk to someone now, the lines in Where to Find Support are free and confidential. You can also browse the doubts and rebuttals on this site, at your own pace.
